utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A brief motion before we continue. I would like to address the Chamber, and I think Mr. Borovic has something to raise briefly too. It's about the next witness we have lined up. This is the witness that was interviewed yesterday, Mr. Korica. I spoke to my learned friends and I think there's a chance that Simic might be done today; however, it wasn't before mid-morning today that I got Korica's interview. I started going through it; it's about two hours and 15 minutes long. He's now having lunch. I shall keep on going for at least another one and a half hours, I will be listening to the tape and perhaps get a chance to talk to him. We're just listening for the time being. If there's any time left today, this man is aged 70 and he has heart problems, therefore I think it might be a good idea to start with him tomorrow as previously envisaged. Therefore, what I'm really raising is that should we be finishing Mr. Simic today, I don't think it would be a good idea to start Mr. Korica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will finish Mr. Simic today, then, and we will then adjourn and we will resume tomorrow afternoon at 2.15 with Mr. Korica. Does that make you happy, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is helpful for everyone, since all my other colleagues have just received the tape. They probably would like to familiarise themselves with that, and I still have to submit the proofing notes to Mr. Moore and I think we can all use tomorrow morning to do some extra work on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: First task, Mr. Lukic, is to finish Simic today. Early, that will give you more time. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to be as brief as possible. This is not about the witness. You imposed a deadline on the OTP about Witness P018, P024 and the related documents. I would like to see what Mr. Smith has done about it. I received a brief answer which confirms what I have heard already. He did not agree but he asked for the documents to be checked beforehand, and after that, he could give an opinion. All I got from the OTP is that Smith had said that he had not agreed before, whereas your ruling was crystal clear, even the seven days, they have all the telephone numbers, they are in touch with the judges who made those rulings. I think it would only be right for this to be checked, and it's been over 10 days now. Just simply to inform the Chamber if they haven't, so far, but virtually nothing has been done about the checks that Mr. Smith was supposed to run on those documents. If the OTP do not believe that they should do that at all, then I would like to ask the Chamber to make a decision based on what I said the last time round. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, my learned friend has had replies. We have contacted Mr. Smith who is in Cambodia. I think we have replied now twice. I am not dealing specifically with the issue but I am aware of the issue. The reply that was given on both occasions was that Mr. Smith had given no undertakings at all, that he informed Mr. Borovic and his colleagues that should they wish to adduce such evidence, they should go about it in the normal way. That, as far as we were aware, was the way it was left, and Mr. Smith was spoken to twice about this recently, and that is the information that he gave us and we passed it forward to my learned friend. May I say, Mr. Smith did speak to me about it at the time. The view I take about that matter is it is for the Defence to call the evidence, to adduce the evidence, to demonstrate what they say is the truth of the documentation, and Mr. Smith agreed with that and informed the Defence of it. I also seem to remember that there was an order from the Court that the Defence should have -- should reply, I think, within 14 days should they wish to call evidence on that matter. But that is from the top of my head. I will have the matters checked, and with the Court's leave, may I deal with it, or perhaps Mr. Lunny, who is dealing with it, deal with it at the start of the next session. I hope it should not take any length of time at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. To be brutally frank, Mr. Moore, I didn't see this coming from you. You have the mail that we sent Mr. Smith based on his own request. Just for ease of handling and in order to make possible better communication with the bodies in Serbia, the authorities there, we worked together in a very respectful manner for a number of years, and now this is the very first time that you are telling the Chamber that Mr. Smith actually did something else. I'm in the hands of the Chamber. The Chamber has my position on these documents. If they don't want that, or if they really mean to challenge their authenticity, the documents are there and it's only a matter of procedure as to what they'll do next. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour allow me just to read a document that was sent to the Defence. I now have it in front of me. It's a very short reply. It was sent by e-mail on the 11th of October, 10.00 in the morning to Ms. Guduric, who is Mr. Borovic's assistant. It reads as follows: "As per my earlier e-mail, Mr. Smith has confirmed that after you asked him to agree the documents and provided contact details, Mr. Smith considered the position and then spoke to you directly to confirm that the documents were not to be agreed. Mr. Smith has confirmed that. He confirmed that he has explained to you that no contact was made with authorities in the former Yugoslavia and that you should proceed to prove the documents for P024 in the normal way by leading evidence. "Mr. Smith has also confirmed that he made no undertaking in relation to Witness P018. I hope this clarifies matters. The Prosecution's position remains the same. No undertaking was given to agree to any of the documents and that the Defence of Mr. Radic was advised of this at the conclusion of the Prosecution case. And then regards, signed by Mr. Lunny." And that has been our position throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The last time the ball is back to you, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour. Your Honours, as for these documents in relation to Witness P018, that's the only thing that's right; there was no undertaking by Mr. Smith. But that is not what lies at the heart of the matter. Neither does the matter that concerns P022. However, as for P024, I think it will be material for OTP. I'm not going into the specific documents now, but I'm sure that had they been interested, they would have checked the authenticity of those documents in the first place. I really have to control myself in order not to overreach myself and say something I might regret, but Mr. Smith never said anything like that and it was just a waste of time for me. Mr. Smith is a very serious person. He never explained from the OTP why I sent an e-mail with all the addresses of the Belgrade courts, the telephone numbers of the judges there. I didn't do that just because I like doing it. Do they get the e-mail or not? On the other hand, this is a witness who apparently duped the OTP. I'm saying "duped the OTP." They didn't check the witness's legitimacy, and this is a problem of a different magnitude than it might work against the OTP, which of course they don't necessarily have to agree with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... At the next -- after the next break. Could the witness now be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Simic. May I remind you of the affirmation that you made at the beginning of your evidence which still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I think Mr. Bulatovic was in the course of asking you questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Simic. We'll continue your examination where we left off yesterday. I do have to ask you one thing, Mr. Simic, after each of my questions, please hold your breath, wait a couple of seconds and please speak slowly in order to give the interpreters a fair chance of interpreting the proceedings. Mr. Simic, on the 19th of November, 1991, you arrived in the hospital area in Vukovar. Do you remember if there were any other officers present there? Can you please describe any memories that you might have about the presence of other officers there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived at the hospital with the company at about 1400 hours. At the main gate, I was met by my battalion commander, Captain First Class Radoje Paunovic. In addition to him, I also met Major Tesic in the hospital, the commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion. He was there with some of his men and he had set up some sort of a security system for the hospital. In addition to Tesic, I also met Major Sljivancanin. Immediately upon our arrival, Captain Paunovic addressed me and gave me some tasks in relation to the hospital security.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, please answer my question. Let's take it one step at a time. Now, did you get any sort of information from Mr. Tesic since you say that he was there setting up a security system already with some of his men? Did he tell you anything about their presence when he had arrived, what he had done, up to that point or anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Tesic told me that he, together with his men, had inspected most of the hospital and that quantities of weapons had been found within the hospital compound. He said there was still a likelihood that some of the people inside the hospital were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What exactly did Paunovic tell you to do?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A police and military task, textbook one. I was told to secure the building. The assignment was given. It contained certain details that I now don't remember. What I remember is that I went with my subordinates to inspect the barracks. I looked at the entire area. I looked at what the buildings and facilities there were, the installations, and then we also looked at the buildings close to the fence which were places at which security elements might have been at risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you said the barracks. I think that's probably a slip of the tongue on your part. You mean the hospital, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed I do, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So did you set up a security system there? If so, please describe what sort of security and how many men did that take?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before we organised security, we used part of the company to partially search the hospital perimeter. We found about three or four rifles. I don't remember the exact number though. After that, we set up a security system. There was reception, there were patrols, there were guards. We appointed a security commander. We had guards, the usual sort of thing that you have in situations like these. You asked me about the numbers. I said yesterday that there were a total of 48 soldiers. In order to set up the entire security system, we needed about 40 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you mentioned the fact that Major Tesic had told you about weapons that had been found. He said there was a danger that some of the people inside the hospital might still be armed. Did you know anything to indicate who it was that was still inside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our information indicated that there were civilians inside the hospital, first and foremost, who had taken shelter there. There were still medical staff, patients, as well as disguised members of Croat paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you were outside the hospital, did you speak to Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We exchanged greetings when I came, but before he left, he drew my attention to everything that I've been telling you about. Particularly he pointed out that there was a possibility that disguised members of Croat paramilitary units were hiding inside and he said we still didn't know, at this point, if they were armed or not. He said I should pay special attention to preserving the lives of my own men, above all. He said I should see to it that I accomplished my mission but that I should focus on preserving the lives of my men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said "before he left." What exactly do you mean when you say that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was still natural light, and before dark, Major Sljivancanin left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of November, did you see anyone from the International Red Cross, anyone from the European community? Did you see any foreign representatives there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that well. There was a team that came, an ICRC team, and when they came, there was this man who led the delegation. I know his first name was Nicholas. He spoke to Major Sljivancanin. I was standing some way from them. I saw them talk, but I don't know what they talked about. At the time I was talking to another person who was the driver --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Just slow down slightly, please.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So while Mr. Sljivancanin, Major Sljivancanin was talking to this gentleman, I was standing at a distance of about 30 metres from them talking to the driver belonging to that delegation who happened to be a Serb from Lika, so we exchanged some words.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about this Nicholas, do you remember how long he stayed at the hospital for?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know they didn't linger for too long. It was soon after this conversation that he had with Major Sljivancanin that they left. I didn't see them after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, can you please describe the atmosphere at the hospital? You said there were civilians there, hospital staff, people. What was the atmosphere like?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was like this: There were a large number of civilians in the hospital building itself. Secondly, outside the hospital perimeter, there were quite a number of people, relatively speaking. There were those that I will term curiosity seekers, there was some TO men from Vukovar, there were volunteers, there were locals who came to look for their own relatives and were waiting for everyone to leave the hospital so that they might check whether their relatives and friends were still alive. There were quite a number of people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, on the 19th, do you remember if there was an evacuation of civilians from the hospital that occurred on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that civilians were evacuated. As far as I know, everyone with the exception of the patients and the hospital staff was allowed to leave the hospital. They left the hospital and the evacuation went on until late in the evening. It got dark very early that time of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What was your concrete task related to the security of the hospital? What were you supposed to secure the hospital from?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The task was a twofold one. First, to prevent uninvited persons from entering the compound and the hospital itself. And secondly, once the evacuation is over, to prevent possible armed provocations from inside and outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, do you remember, while you were securing the hospital on the 19th of November, did anybody else enter the hospital apart from the people that you mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The building itself, only a foreign TV crew entered the hospital during the course of the day, no one else. No members of the brigade or any other unit entered the hospital in an unauthorised way. The TV crew had the proper permit to come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this foreign TV crew? Did they come on their own or did somebody bring them?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The clue did not come on their own, because the crew was brought by Captain Maric. I knew Captain Maric because for a while, he worked in the 2nd Battalion of the military police at Mount Avala, and I know that he had been wounded or injured during combat operations; I'm not sure. Then when I saw him alive and well, I was really happy. That's how I remember that he was there, in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain, Mr. Simic, whether this presence of Captain Maric influenced you in terms of allowing the TV crew to enter the hospital, since your assignment was not to allow anyone to enter the hospital or did this motivate you to let them in?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first when I saw them at the gate, I exchanged greetings with Maric. I asked him whether these people had a permit --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've let it go so far but there's no reference at all in any of the three summaries about Captain Maric. There is a reference to a TV crew, but there's no mention about Maric and there's no mention about conversations. Unless I'm wrong, and I don't believe I am, I object to that aspect of the evidence. Perhaps we've heard now three summaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Moore is right, Your Honours. Indeed, I never mentioned that, who the TV crew came with, but since he talked about the foreign TV crew coming, I thought that I could ask that, too, but that is not really that important, so perhaps I can move on to another subject and other matters at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how long that crew stayed at the hospital, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you exactly. Captain Maric and I were standing, or rather sitting, or rather standing in front of the entrance, and then when they left, we saw them off.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: During your stay there on the 19th, was your commander present there, of the 2nd Battalion of the military police, Mr. Paunovic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the time of my arrival to the hospital, he was with me throughout that time. However -- well, I don't know now. Around 5.00 or 5.30, he went to the command of the Guards Brigade to the briefing there. After the briefing, I think he came back two hours later or perhaps it was a bit more than that. Then he was with us until after midnight. Sometime after midnight he went back, or rather he went back to his command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All the time from his return to -- from the briefing until he went to the command post, were you together all the time or did you go somewhere in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go anywhere from the hospital compound, but from time to time, I did go to see the security organs, to talk to people. There were quite a few other obligations that I had there as company commander. The soldiers had to be taken care of properly in terms of where they'd spend the night, then their food and so on. There are many things that I had to deal with as company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: As for security matters, did you discuss anything with Mr. Paunovic, the commander, before he went to the briefing? Do you remember having discussed anything with him?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we analysed the situation, and primarily in view of the fact that we were securing a facility that we were unfamiliar with, there was this assumption and possibility that within the hospital, there were unarmed people -- there were armed people, rather. When we saw how many people we had in our own company, on the one hand, the company has certain duties regarding this security. In this discussion, I proposed to the commander that if it is possible, to get some people from other companies and battalions that we reinforce my company, because at that moment, we did not know how long this security task would last and the unit was involved in searches on that day. They had been through a long march and the soldiers were really exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Paunovic respond to these suggestions of yours?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he was going to the briefing and that at the briefing he would explain the situation and that he will ask for approval, permission to reinforce the 4th Company with personnel from some other unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say that you saw him when he came back from the briefing. Did he say something to you in relation to your previous conversation, whether he had talked about anything at the command, whether he had any new information for you in terms of reinforcing the security there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon his return, he said that his proposal was -- had been accepted, and that we would get reinforcements from the 1st Company. Since it was night-time, it was not possible to do it straight away, but he told me to wait until the morning and that Lieutenant Todorovic would bring part of his soldiers there to reinforce my company. On that occasion, that is to say, after his return, he told me that on the following day, an evacuation would be carried out, both of patients and medical staff. And on that occasion, he told me what I, as company commander, should do on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Major Karan is?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Major Mladen Karan was a desk officer in the security department of the Guards Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see him in the hospital on the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when he came and why?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think around 1900 hours, he came and said that he had orders to take Dr. Vesna Bosanac to Negoslavci. We came to the entrance together. We called Dr. Bosanac. She went out. We told her that she was supposed to go to Negoslavci. She told us to wait so that she could get some of her personal belongings. She left and came back very quickly. I remember she had this little bag with her. And then with Major Karan, she went to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, does the name Marin Vidic, Bili, mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the name, but I really don't know what his position was. I know that on that very same evening, on the 19th, that is, when I returned from my tour of the security organs, I stopped at the desk again. The soldier who worked at the reception desk told me that the commander battalion had been there and he took a man from the hospital, that they drove off. When Captain Paunovic came back, he told me that this person who he took was Marin Vidic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: To avoid any confusion, Mr. Paunovic --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry about that. As for your contacts with Mr. Paunovic, let us clarify some matters. If I understand you correctly, you were with Paunovic until 1730 hours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: After that, if I understand you correctly, Paunovic went to the briefing and came back two hours later in your estimate, which is to say around 2000 hours.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let us clarify this. He came back from the briefing. He took Marin Vidic, returned to Negoslavci, and went back to the hospital yet again. It is only when he returned to the hospital yet again that I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what confused me a bit. That's what I wanted to clarify. And then when he returned from Negoslavci, how long did Mr. Paunovic stay in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He left the hospital sometime around midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Simic, I'm interested in the atmosphere that prevailed around the hospital. You mentioned the presence of some volunteers, territorials, local people, what was the atmosphere like? Was there any attacks, assaults, was there any aggressive behaviour vis-a-vis the people you were securing who were staying at the hospital? Can you describe that at bit?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, these people who were around the hospital were not within the compound; they were out in the street. Part of these people were verbally provoking, abusing my security organs saying things along the lines of: You're guarding Ustashas, my brother's killer's there, my father's killer's there. And that's where it all ended, these verbal provocations. As night fell, most of these people left. When the evacuation of all these civilians was over, everything became quiet. From 8.00 onwards, really, there weren't any provocations. Everything was peaceful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: These provocations and these things that these people did from outside the hospital that you talked about, do you think that they endangered the people in the hospital? Were they that dangerous? Did they really constitute a threat for the people in the hospital and for you, too, because you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not, because our task was that if this went beyond verbal provocations, we would have reacted. There weren't any indicators that showed that something could happen to the people who were there. On the basis of our assessment of the behaviour of these people, we saw that the bottom line was these verbal provocations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Page 16, line 19 in the transcript, you said 8.00 when everything became quiet, is this 8.00 in the morning or 8.00 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, in addition to this TV crew that entered the hospital on the 19th, do you remember whether anybody else entered the hospital, got out of the hospital, except for these civilians that you mentioned? After 8.00 in the evening, did anybody go into the hospital or out of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, nobody entered the hospital. According to the reports of my security organs and according to what I saw myself, no one entered the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, let us now move on to what happened on the 20th. You had information from Paunovic, as you said, that on the next day, there would be an evacuation of the sick and wounded and people who had stayed on at the hospital. Did he give you any details on the evening of the 19th concerning this evacuation, or did he just say there's going to be an evacuation and you're going to have certain tasks and then describe these tasks?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He ordered me to prepare about 10 soldiers, I don't remember the exact figure, I think it's 10, whose task it would be to search people. Further on, I was told that the evacuation would most probably start at 8.00 in the morning, as far as I can remember, and that I should assign about two soldiers who would perhaps be there if anybody tried to do anything, I mean these people who were being searched.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. This search, this frisking, is it a complex, complicated procedure? Could you explain this procedure of frisking persons who are supposed to be evacuated, from the point of view of military police work?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very simple procedure. It's very simple work. I don't know if I need to describe all the details now, how this is actually done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm just interested in the nature of this activity. Is it simple?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a simple activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Paunovic told you that reinforcements would come on the following day in relation to the evacuation and everything else and now I'm asking you whether these reinforcements came?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the morning. Lieutenant Todorovic brought people from the 1st Company of the military police so our company was reinforced. I think there were about 20 soldiers who came as a reinforcement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On that morning, did you see Mr. Sljivancanin; if so, when? Did you see him coming to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin came to the hospital in the morning. It was around 7.00 or 7.30. He came with another group of officers. We exchanged greetings as he came in. He asked me whether there had been any problems in the night and I said that everything was fine, and then with this group of officers he went on into the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what do you conclude, Mr. Simic, that these were officers?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they wore uniforms, and I saw that they had rank insignia. I cannot say what rank, because I only exchanged greetings with Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How many people were there with Major Sljivancanin; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think there were four or five persons, but a bit later, yet another group of officers came. I just asked: Who are you? And they said that they were doctors. I think there were four or five of them too. And then they entered the hospital as well. The doctors also wore uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you that. I asked you something different. On the 20th, from the morning, from that moment of Veselin Sljivancanin's arrival with a group of officers, did you enter the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So we can agree, Mr. Simic, that you don't know what was being done in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th, was your battalion commander there too, Mr. Paunovic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battalion commander arrived a little later, but he spent most of the day within the hospital perimeter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, before I move on to these specific actions that you took, searching people there and whatever you did, let me ask you something else. On the 19th of November, you see Mr. Sljivancanin, you describe your conversation with him. On the 20th of November, you see Mr. Sljivancanin, you describe your conversation with him. On the 19th or the 20th, did Mr. Sljivancanin give you any orders?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I took my orders from the battalion commander, Captain Paunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, perhaps, see Veselin Sljivancanin give any orders to Mr. Paunovic, the battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I noticed. I really can't say, but not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say your task was to search persons. When did you start, and tell us about the progress of this task?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime after the group of officers had entered the hospital, persons started leaving. I know someone was actually leading them away two by two, I think. A group of about 50 people was formed. We got them lined up. I walked up to them and said: Anyone with any blunt objects on them or possibly firearms -- or, rather, just across the way from that group, there were several tables so that they should lay down their blunt objects or implements of firearms on those tables. None of those persons were armed. There were about 10 soldiers and about 50 of those. And each soldier had to search five persons. They would search these people individually. Once the soldiers were done, I would tell them to stand on the right and then we would escort this group as far as the hospital entrance where buses were waiting for them. People would get onto these buses and I would walk back. There was another group of persons to be searched lined up for us in the meantime, and it just went on like that, over and over.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say you took them to that bus, told them to stand on the right. Once people left the exit, were the buses facing left or facing right from the exit? I do not wish to tire you with this, Mr. Simic. Let's not waste time. We have photographs to show that.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left, you're leaving the hospital, or right, so the buses were on the left. In that passage, that's where the people were who were being searched.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Just give me the distance between the buses and the hospital exit, please.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exit to the gate must be between 50 and 100 metres at most.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say that you with your soldiers who had searched these persons escorted these persons who had been searched. Did you do that every time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I just did that with the first group. As soon as I escorted the first group out, I realised that Major Vukasinovic would say there. We exchanged greetings. I know him because he used to be the battalion commander before Captain Paunovic came along, and the hand-over actually occurred about one or two months previously. He met those people there. There was really no need to meet them. They walked in a column, and they were just getting on those buses one by one. As for those other groups, there was no need for me to follow them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing the number of the bus that was parked in the place where you brought those people?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you how many buses there were. These buses came to get these people on that day, and then the evacuation buses came later on for the remaining medical staff. So, believe me, I really can't say how many buses there were exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if any military policemen were escorting those buses?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were soldiers securing the buses, inside the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were those soldiers from your company?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't. Even if I wanted to, I simply had no soldiers at the time to assign to that escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what company they were from?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what became of the soldiers that Lieutenant Todorovic had brought there, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know what became of those from Todorovic's company that he had handed over to me as reinforcement. But I don't know how many soldiers he had brought to begin with or what these soldiers were eventually used for.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: These persons you searched, were these persons able to walk or not?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them were able to walk.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice any of them sporting any bandages or something like that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were about 10 people, probably, with bandages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find any weapons on these persons?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I have already said in my statement, the only person who spoke up was a barber who said that he had some barber's kit on him and he asked me whether he should lay that down too. I said he would be expected to, so he just put it down on one of those tables over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What was the purpose of this search? What exactly did you want to establish by doing that? Why is a thing like that done?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The principle and sole purpose of that search was to establish whether any of these persons had any blunt objects on them or perhaps firearms. Were any to be found, they would be seized.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said the only person with any sort of kit on them was the barber which he then laid down. What I want to know is, did you take personal documents away from these people that you searched, any valuables, any personal belongings such as money or jewellery?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing whatsoever was seized from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you say you never actually went into the hospital and you didn't know what was going on there. Do you perhaps know, and if so how, whether any sort of a triage was conducted inside the hospital before the people were sent outside to be searched by your men?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose there would have had to be some sort of a triage because not everybody left, and a lot of people were late.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th, do you remember any ICRC people at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same man who had appeared on the previous day named Nicholas came again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what time it was when he came? Was it during your search, if we can use that as a reference point?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was after the search, after the search had already been concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How long after?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he might have arrived at about 11.00, but I think we had already completed all of our tasks by this time, but 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did he speak to anyone there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't see. He must have spoken to someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see anyone else from any other organisation there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from them, I think there was an international community team. They wore those arm bands with the European community emblem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, did you see the buses leave and when?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be certain. When my job was done, I withdrew. I wasn't responsible for the buses so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say you saw Major Vukasinovic, you know him and you explained why. Did you see any other officers next to those buses?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been other officers there, but I don't remember any. The only one I do remember is Major Vukasinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see Major Sljivancanin anywhere around the buses at any time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say that you saw Major Sljivancanin enter the hospital. Did you see him leave the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, it wasn't exactly my assignment to follow Major Sljivancanin. I can't say whether he came or went or how often and how long he stayed for.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see him on the 20th outside the hospital within the perimeter? Did you see him doing anything in particular, or were you just not paying attention?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wasn't paying attention to that. We weren't really in touch that much. I should assume that he was just doing his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If you notice Sljivancanin or any of his activities outside the hospital, did you, perhaps, see him trying to prevent anyone at all from entering the hospital in any way at all, barring access to the hospital to anyone at all?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember noticing anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You talked about the presence of the TO men on the 19th. Were they there on the 20th as well?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not within the hospital perimeter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about outside the perimeter?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say. Maybe they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If so, did you perhaps notice any kind of aggressive behaviour by them against the people that you were escorting or searching?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None that I noticed. All I can tell you is that our job was done in a virtually perfect and very professional manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Mr. Simic, you're searching those people, right, people on their way out of the hospital. You're taking them to those buses. During all of this time, did anyone at all try to physically attack those persons being searched in front of the buses or indeed harm them in any way?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any sufficient manpower to prevent any such attacks?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had 48 men, as I have said before. There were about 20 men there from the 1st Company which adds up to a total of about 70 men. I think that that number of men should be sufficient to stop any taunts or threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This is a hypothetical question, but let me try to phrase it this way. On the 19th or the 20th, if those groups had tried anything serious such as penetrating the hospital or attacking those people, you, as the commander of that security group, what would you have done? Which steps would you have taken?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My principal assignment was to secure the people inside the hospital. If anything like that had happened, I would have done everything within my power and within my authority. There are 14 different types of powers that police have. First, we would warn any such people trying to attack the hospital or people. The next would be to use fire-power or physical force. One thing is certain, we would have done everything within our power to keep those people from being harmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say that in your estimation, the evacuation took about two hours. Was there another evacuation that followed?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was another evacuation of all the people still remaining in the hospital: The wounded, the patients, medical staff. Eventually, there was still some of the medical staff left inside the hospital, those who opted to stay, as well as those patients who refused to move. Most people had been taken away. I spent most of my time at the entrance, the emergency ward. I left some of my soldiers there just in case of need. When the wounded and patients were being brought in, it was quite high up and just in order to help them stretcher those people into the hospital, medical assistance, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, once your mission was accomplished, did you submit any sort of reports to anyone?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the time the battalion commander was there with me. Needless to say, once this was all over, I reported to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: A verbal report or a written report?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A verbal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any observations made about your report to the effect that you had omitted to do something?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the simple reason being it was a very professional job.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, did you take any notes about all of these steps that you took about all of your assignments?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As any other officer, I kept a war notebook, a war logbook in which I recorded everything that I received from my superior officer as well as any orders that I imparted to my subordinates, or anything else, for that matter, that struck me as important or typical.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you say there was an evacuation that followed, the one of the wounded patients and medical staff. What I want to know is after this evacuation, did you do any other searches or checks in order to see what the situation was inside the hospital and around it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The evacuation went on until past 1600 hours and it got dark very soon, so we didn't do anything else on that day. However, the next day, we did a thorough search of the hospital, the hospital where those people were, as well as all those other buildings, and we thoroughly searched the hospital perimeter, the entire area of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find anything?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on that occasion, we found relatively large quantities of weapons, starting with automatic rifles; there were over 20 of them. Then there were hunting guns. Then there were pistols. Then different types of knives. I can tell you that I, myself, at the entrance where the emergency ward was, there was this heap of sand. When we looked through that sand, we found an old rucksack containing over 20 pistols. Also in the immediate vicinity, there were some logs that they probably used as a barrier so that they would protect themselves from shells. We found an automatic rifle there too. We found most automatic weapons in containers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, did you search the hospital inside? Did you find anything there that would be noteworthy?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We searched the hospital in detail, but inside the hospital we didn't find any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What was your impression after you found these weapons? The members of your company, were they indeed endangered? Did the people in the hospital constitute a threat to them?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, obviously the intention was to hide everything that was near the entrance, these weapons, that is, which gives me the right to assume that perhaps somebody wanted the weapons to be close by so that they could grab them as soon as possible. It was rather complex and fear was justified. As we are carrying out this mission, we did not know, for instance, that the new part of the hospital is linked to the old part of the hospital with a tunnel. When we entered the hospital, when we saw that, I realised that, for example, a group of even 100 men could have gone from one part to the other and killed us all from the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You talked about the ethnic composition of your unit, but I'm interested in something else. Did you have any members of the Territorial Defence within your unit?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any members of the so-called reservists in your unit?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who these reservists are, can you explain that to us? We know, perhaps, this system of defence, but maybe the Trial Chamber would like to hear some explanations as to what we mean when we say "reservists"?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an expert in that field, but I'll try to explain this for you. According to the solutions that were then in place, there were two categories of soldiers within the JNA. There were conscripts, who were doing their military service; and there were soldiers who were members of the reserve force. When a person of the male gender completed his military service, he would become part of the reserve force. I think that this goes on until the age of 50, I don't know what the situation is now, or 55. So these are people who had served in the military a term of 12 or 15 months, it varied, but most of these members of the reserve force had done a military service of 12 to 15 months. They completed military training lasting six months. When we're talking about the military police, they were involved in military police work. From the moment when they completed their military service, they were called up for different training exercises, military police work was done, there were shooting exercises and so on and so forth, so these are very well-trained people. Also at that time, our conscripts were 19 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Please speak slower.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Soldiers did their military service at the age of 19. We all know that people of 19 are not mature people; whereas, the reservists were older, mature, in the meantime they had, say, completed university, they were trained, they were healthy. Younger people were selected for military police work, not persons up to the age of 55, so not those who were almost 55. Physically and mentally healthy, well-trained, that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, these are mature persons who had undergone full training. I'm interested in these soldiers who were doing their regular military service who were in your unit. How much training had they received until the 20th? What class are we talking about, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came to do their military service in June that year; that is to say, that they had been trained for about three months before they were taken into combat action.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What is your personal view, this three-month training, is that sufficient for taking people into combat and military police work of this kind? What is your view?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Once again, I've looked at the various summaries. I don't see anything on this topic at all. Perhaps my learned friend could point it to me and which summary, as I have had to do it very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the proofing notes that I submitted to the OTP it does say that this witness is going to talk about the ethnic composition of the unit and also about the reservists, and generally who reservists are. I think that that is within that subject, and I think that this question went beyond what I said to my learned friend by way of this notification. So may I proceed now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: To another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, how long were you engaged in securing the hospital in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My company secured it until they returned to Belgrade; that is to say, until the 24th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And who took over the security of the hospital after you left?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit of the military police from Kragujevac. I think it was the 80th Motorised Brigade, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I omitted to ask you something, I hope you don't mind. These buses on the 20th who were taking people away, the people you had searched, do you know where these buses went? Did anybody tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, my superior officer did not say that to me. I just know that people were talking about it, people who worked there, that there was this possibility of them going to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, nobody told you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody told me officially. I was just told that after the search, I should take people to the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Paunovic -- sorry, Simic, Mr. Simic, I keep thinking of Paunovic as your superior officer. So, Mr. Simic, you were in combat within Assault Detachment 2?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke here about the ethnic composition of your unit, about combat activities. I'm not going to ask you a lot about that because I'm not really interested in that, not that much. Were there any problems in Assault Detachment 2 and, if so, can you explain what they had to do with? Was it refusing to carry out orders, leaving positions, refusing to go into combat? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, in wartime, there are always problems, and there are always problems in terms of command as well. The greatest problem that I had while I was in Assault Detachment 2 was the problem I had on the 4th of November, 1991. I remember that because that is the day of the Guards Motorised Brigade. Colonel Maric, who was assistant commander for morale in the brigade command, toured the units on that day. I know he came to see me. I don't know who else he saw on that day. And he had a meeting with officers and soldiers who were on duty. On that occasion, he congratulated all the soldiers, all the members of the company on the day of this unit, and after a particular -- after this discussion, questions followed. Since during the course of the days right before that, either the Assembly or the government of Serbia had passed a decision that reservists could stay only for 45 days and it was then that their 45 days were up, the 45 days of our reserve force. The logical question put -- was put to Colonel Maric, whether the JNA and the Guards Brigade would honour that decision. Colonel Maric said yes. After that, another question followed: What about the rest of us? Are we going back too? Colonel Maric said yes. On that occasion, I cautioned him that in view of my knowledge, the reservists would be relieved, whereas other officers and soldiers would stay on mission. He then said that what he had said was correct. In the meantime, this information caused a lot of commotion within the unit. I don't know what the situation was in other units, but people started talking that in the morning when the reservists leave, that all the rest would leave with them, and that they would leave their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, did you do anything on account of that? Did you inform your superior officer or whatever?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to find Captain Paunovic. Then I was told that he was most probably at the brigade command. In view of the seriousness of the situation, I took a vehicle and went to Negoslavci. At that moment, a meeting was held, a briefing, I don't know what it was, I know that they didn't let me in straight away. But afterwards, well, there was this small cocktail party, if I can put it that way, on the occasion of the day of the unit, so I walked in and addressed Colonel Mrksic and I told him what the problem was. He replied to me that Colonel Maric would come on the following day and that he would resolve all these problems talking to the soldiers, that it's probably some kind of a misunderstanding, and that it would be resolved. I said to him then that I do not want Colonel Maric to come because he is the one who caused the entire situation. Then he told me to speak to Lieutenant-Colonel Panic. I spoke to Lieutenant-Colonel Panic and I told him what this was all about. He told me that that was not his line of work and that if the commander said that Maric should go, then let Maric go.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: To cut the whole story short, who did what and when, was the problem resolved?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the core of the matter was that I spoke to Sljivancanin then, that he would -- and he said that he would talk to the commander and that he would come in the morning. In the morning, Major Sljivancanin came. Through a professional, responsible discussion with these people, he persuaded these people to remain at the front line and I thank him for that to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This situation that you're talking about now, is that a situation that jeopardised the security and safety of your unit?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. If we leave our position, if armed men with ammunition go away, you cannot have a bigger security problem than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, would it be right to take the break now so that I could have a look at my remaining questions and then bring my examination to a close? I do have a few minutes left, but then perhaps this would be a good point to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the break now, Mr. Bulatovic, and resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, one question that I should have asked before, it's about the 20th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I did indicate that we would deal with another matter after the break, and I was distracted by your presence and forgot about it. Would you mind a moment? That's Mr. Lunny and Mr. Borovic that are mainly concerned. Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Your Honour, I did have the advantage of following the proceedings before the break. I am not sure I can usefully add much beyond what was said by my learned friend, Mr. Moore. The position I would submit is perfectly clear and straightforward. The Prosecution has contacted Mr. Smith. I did so myself, both by e-mail and then by telephone. And in both Mr. Smith's e-mail and during the course of conversation with him, he confirmed the position as was set out in my e-mails to Your Lordship's Chamber and my learned friends earlier last week. Mr. Smith was asked to agree a series of documents in respect of Witness P024. Mr. Smith left to consider that position. He discussed that with Mr. Moore. A decision was then taken that the documents could not be agreed and Mr. Smith then conveyed that in court to Mr. Borovic with Ms. Guduric translating. Mr. Smith was quite clear that his recollection was clear on that point. He did so at the close of the Prosecution case, and he made it perfectly clear to my learned friend that the Prosecution would not check the documents and would not agree the documents and advised Mr. Borovic that should they seek to rely upon them, they should prove them in the normal way in the course of their Defence case. And unless there's anything I can further add, Your Honour, I would submit that the position has been made perfectly clear to Mr. Borovic by my former colleague and learned friend, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. Your Honours, I would like to know if my learned friends care to share that with us. After the e-mail that I sent about links to courts in Serbia, did Mr. Smith check the documents or not after that? I'm very curious. I have never been informed. We are taking up a lot of the Chamber's valuable time. I never received a reply as to whether these documents were checked or not. Why would I even be bothering the Chamber with this? I was truly astonished that someone came to testify here, the person who was a common criminal, lying to the Prosecution. There is an international arrest warrant against this person and the OTP are protecting him and sheltering him. I think this is something that definitely deserves the attention of the Trial Chamber. Were Articles 54 and 89 appropriately interpreted by the OTP or the Defence. There are written submissions about this. It's down to the Chamber to judge that. You have been very patient with us, Your Honours, you've given us an opportunity to submit our positions. It is now, I would submit, down to the Chamber to be the judge of this matter and to see who is right and who is wrong. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would understand, Mr. Borovic, that the answer to the question you posed is "no." That's what I understood from the submissions that were put by Mr. Moore and Mr. Lunny, and I detect nods of agreement. This matter is the subject of a motion before the Chamber and we will now continue our consideration of the merits. Thank you. Now, Mr. Borovic -- Mr. Bulatovic, I'm sorry to have interrupted you. Would you please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour, with Your Honour's leave, may I now withdraw from Court and hand it back to my friend, Mr. Moore. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I hope that after this altercation where sparks were flying we can now resume a calmer tone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I should have asked you this before, Mr. Simic, but oversights are always possible. The morning of the 20th, you are conducting this certain, persons are being led away from the hospital, you search them, and then they are taken to the buses. Is all of this something that Veselin Sljivancanin is involved in?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you provided a number of different statements about the circumstances. How many exactly?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Who did you provide these statements to and when?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave a statement to the military court. I believe this was early in 1999. I also provided a statement to the court trying the Ovcara case in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: July last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. When you provided those statements -- first the military court, right? What about the investigating magistrate who took your statement? Did he show you any document for you to look at or did you just tell the story as you then remembered it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement was based on my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about the statement in June or, rather, on the 6th of July, your statement to the special department of the district court for war crimes in Belgrade, which is often referred to as the Special War Crimes Tribunal. On that occasion, did any of those involved in asking you questions show you any sort of document at all?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand the question. Is this about my evidence in court?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I was shown at the time were photographs of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The last question that concludes my examination, it's a question that everybody likes to ask: As far as your recollection of all of these events was concerned, when was it freshest, when was it clearest or best?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Needless to say, my recollection was clearest after these events, immediately after these events. However, once I found out that I would be testifying at this Tribunal, given the importance of the Tribunal and this particular trial, I conducted a lot of conversations with my fellow soldiers who were involved in these events. I also met Counsel Lukic twice, possibly a third time, and I was also proofed in The Hague. During the proofing sessions, I was shown many video clips which brought back everything that I had struggled to suppress, a number of unpleasant memories.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And just to wrap this up, who proofed you in The Hague after your arrival in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was you who proofed me after my arrival in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I am attorney-at-law Vladimir Domazet, one of Mr. Mrksic's counsel. I will be asking you a couple of questions. A while ago, you were talking about your previous statements. I hope that as you were being proofed you had occasion to refresh your memory about your 1999 statement and your evidence at the Belgrade Ovcara trial. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said a while ago that both times, you testified based on your recollection, for the most part, right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You probably don't have these statements on you; therefore, I would kindly ask the usher to hand you these two statements and to provide copies for the Trial Chamber as well in English. We have both the B/C/S and the English here. If necessary, you can consult these statements. I will be telling you which paragraphs to look at. But first, let me ask you something else: You talked about taking orders from your commander. You mentioned his name a couple of times. Sometimes you didn't. I suppose all you said about that was in reference to your commander, Paunovic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean that you addressed him whenever you had problems carrying out any tasks or assignments received from him or your other superiors? What was the procedure whenever you came across problems such as the ones in relation to those civilians around the hospital or when searching the Mitnica location, any sort of problem at all, who would you go to for instructions?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever I came across problems while going about my tasks, I would go to my direct superior. Throughout my time in Vukovar, there were several people who were my direct superiors. Speaking about what you asked me about, of course I would have gone to the battalion commander, Captain Paunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You say several different superior officers at different times, I suppose, you are talk being your own direct superior, right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was always the chain of command, wasn't there? If I had been resubordinated to the Armoured Battalion, then its commander would have been my superior. When I was part of Assault Detachment 2, my superior officer was Lieutenant-Colonel Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would it have been the done thing, or usual, if you like? Has it ever happened to you that there was a problem and yet you failed to inform your superior officer, informing instead the deputy or the commander of Operations Group or his deputy, the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever the battalion commander was away, I explained a while ago that I wasn't able to locate the battalion commander. In that case, I would have spoken be to the next officer in command, the second in command with a view to resolving any trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So the normal procedure would have been to go to your direct superior officer, right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You talked about the time you arrived at the hospital grounds on the 19th of November. Today you said that this happened at about 1400 hours?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You can go back to your previous statements, you can have a look to see that in 1999, you said it was about 14, 1500 hours and last year you said it was between 1500 hours and 1600 hours. What you said today, does that not follow from your previous answer, that you consulted someone or looked at some documents so you decided that it was about 1400 hours, or is your memory fresher now or was your memory fresher before? Can you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Last year on the 2nd of July I returned after a three-month stay abroad. I went directly to the courtroom, in a manner of speaking. I hadn't even had time to go through my previous statement to the military court. Believe me, I spoke to other people in Belgrade who were with me, and we concluded, since there was this dilemma concerning 1400 hours or 1500 hours, that 1400 hours would be the most realistic estimate, in terms of time, and our arrival there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. That's understandable.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, we didn't hear the speakers. Could they please kindly be asked to both speak -- to not speak at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You say you never entered the hospital but you were informed about the persons inside the hospital and then you told us who those people were. Among other things, there were some people you were told that were inside the hospital who were suspected of being armed and possible members of Croat paramilitary units. What I want to know is: Who told you this, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you during my evidence today that Major Tesic was the one who told me about that as one of the possibilities. So did my own commander. I believe Major Sljivancanin said the same thing, that there was a likelihood that there were still members inside and that possibly they were still armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. You spoke about that afternoon, the 19th. You were deploying your soldiers around the hospital. How long did the whole operation take until a security system was finally in place?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly, but I know that by nightfall the deployment of the entire security detail had been concluded. I mean internally, within the company, and everything else. So by nightfall --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note the witness trails off.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. The response to one of Mr. Bulatovic's questions today, you said that your direct superior officer, Paunovic, had gone to Negoslavci for that briefing at about 5.00 or 5.30 that afternoon. Do you remember in your previous statements whether you ever referred to that, his departure that afternoon for that briefing at the command?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. It's not a detail that I remember. I don't remember if I said that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We'll come to that. What I want to know is: Did you, perhaps, just remember that? Was your memory jogged or perhaps somebody told you, just as somebody told you about the time line; or is this something that you remember, that you've always remembered, but you just simply didn't say it back in 1999 or in your other statement?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but in both my previous statements, I was answering questions. I was asked questions and I answered specific questions that I was asked. I should assume that if I was ever asked about this, I probably would have answered it, wouldn't I?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you please go to your statement dated 1999, page 3; the English reference is page 4, lines 22 through 26. For you, it's the lower half of page 3 where it says the tasks of -- the task of securing the hospital. And then the next sentence it starts: "However ..."

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 3. What exactly did you say, how does that begin?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: "However, there were a lot of people on the hospital grounds." Have you got that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. It might take some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This is the lower half of the page, the second last paragraph. It starts "the next day," just underneath, four lines down: "However, there were a lot of people on the hospital grounds." Have you found that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I looking at the right document?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You have --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day, it could have been on the 20th of November, the persons we were taking outside the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, four lines before that.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "However, there were a lot of people on the hospital grounds."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Slowly, please. Please read all the way to the end of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
