utterances.text: "However, there were a lot of people on the hospital grounds, civilians, inhabitants, so the officers from the brigade command organised this, and I think Major Sljivancanin was in charge for them to leave the hospital and to walk away from the hospital compound. They left, and this was completed by 19 or 2000 hours."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My question: Who walked away from the hospital compound? Did you mean the civilians or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier today that on that day, all persons who weren't medical staff or patients were allowed to leave the hospital. That's what I'm saying. On that day, people were leaving the hospital. I said earlier told that during the night, or during the dark, people were still leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Are you talking about hospital patients leaving the hospital or are you talking about somebody else leaving?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that all persons who were not hospital staff or patients were allowed to leave the hospital on the afternoon of the 19th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just in order to be fair to the witness, I think it might be a good idea for my learned friend Mr. Domazet, because he's allowing the witness to read out an entire paragraph from a statement, and this specifies what people we are talking about. There is no reference to hospital patients, so I think he's trying to insinuate that these are the people we are talking about, whereas there is no reference to that. The statement is clear. There were quite a number of people, civilians and inhabitants, but there is no mention there of any patients. Therefore, I don't quite understand the purpose of this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Your Honour, I will try to explain. I didn't mean the patients. I didn't say this was about the patients or that they were leaving the hospital. That's precisely what the witness said. I don't understand this. I never heard that. He talked about the 19th and about people leaving the hospital. So it was my understanding, based on this, that he was talking about people who were on the hospital grounds, civilians, and that's why I asked, and that's what I would like to ask you to have a look and to focus and to try to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you uttered this sentence, who exactly did you have in mind? Who are the persons leaving the hospital compound on foot, walking away?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you look in my statement, you can see that this is about civilians, inhabitants of Vukovar who happened to be in the hospital. On that day, that afternoon, the 19th, late afternoon, they were allowed to leave the Vukovar Hospital, which they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Fair enough. When you say that this was organised by officers from the brigade command, which officers did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "officers from the brigade command," I mean Major Sljivancanin. Were there several of them or not, I don't know. I know Major Sljivancanin was there. I said earlier today that this was organised and that he then left. I said he left before nightfall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But you said there were officers who organised this. That's plural, isn't it? So I'm not asking you about Sljivancanin. I'm asking you about any other officers belonging to the brigade who were there. Did you have anybody else in mind?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him. I'm not sure if there was anybody else with him. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said before nightfall, and here you say that the whole thing was over by 1900 hours or 2000 hours. Do we agree that night falls much earlier in November, that time of the year. So it cannot be that both are true. Although in the English, the only reference we see is 1900 hours; but in the Serbian, we see the time frame specified as between 19 and 2000 hours.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I have a distinct impression that you misunderstand me. In these statements, in my evidence today, I said that on the 19th the civilians who were evacuated from the hospital were still being evacuated for about an hour or two after nightfall. I think you heard me. And the hospital staff and all the other people there that were evacuated on the 20th were evacuated by 1600 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I heard you loud and clear in relation to the 20th, but now we are talking about the 19th, so let's stick to the 19th. What do you remember about that afternoon, the afternoon of the 19th, or the late afternoon/early evening of the 19th?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The idea was that there were 2.000 to 3.000 people in the hospital. That is what was assumed. I think that I am repeating this for the third time, that that day, on the 19th, in the afternoon and in the evening, the inhabitants of Vukovar who happened to be there had the possibility to leave, and only the medical staff and the patients would remain in the hospital. Now these persons, these civilians went out, perhaps until 1900 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. If that's your explanation, I'll accept it. So you've clarified the matter. You talked about the order issued by your commander, Mr. Paunovic, to search persons. You talked about these 10 soldiers who were supposed to be singled out for that. When did you receive this order from your commander?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, while giving evidence today, that this was after Paunovic returned from the briefing, or, rather, in the meantime, he took Marin Vidic away and he returned by around 8.00. When he returned, he told me that we received approval to reinforce forces for securing the hospital and also he ordered me to search these persons tentatively around 8.00 in the morning. That's what he said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said today that one of the reasons why he went to the briefing was that he would ask for these reinforcements; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just asking for reinforcements within your unit of the military police, was that something that was supposed to be presented at the briefing or could he have resolved that within his own units, the units that he commanded or anybody else's? Do you believe that it had to be brought up at a meeting like this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presented the problem to my commander. Now, whether he's going to resolve it on his own or whether he is going to present it to the commander of the brigade at the briefing is up to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My question is whether he could have ordered the reinforcement of the unit on his own? You talked about that --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Theoretically, he could have resolved it on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you said that he went to the briefing, that you saw him afterwards, about two hours later, but that you did not see him at the moment when he came back and when he took Marin Vidic away or only -- you actually only saw him after he came back from taking Marin Vidic away.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So I can assume that you heard that from somebody else, that he took Marin Vidic away and that he then came back.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in my statement that I was touring my security organs and that I went out to regulate the night-rest of my soldiers. When I came back to the reception desk, the soldier there told me that the commander was there and that he took a man away. Who that person was, I found out when Captain Paunovic came back yet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. Could you please look at the minutes from Ovcara, page 5 of the Serbian version; the English version is page 8. The transcript didn't say that the B/C/S is page 5 and that English is page 8. Have you found the page?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, page 5, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So your answer to the question put by the president of the chamber, perhaps I can read it out and you will tell me whether I read it out right, what it says in that statement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note we do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: "For the most part during that night, I was at the reception desk at the main entrance. For quite a while, the battalion commander was there together with me. That's where we were. Quite simply, you come there and you secure a facility that you see for the first time. There were relatively few of us. We did not have information as to who was inside, whether there was anybody who was armed or unarmed, and for that reason, practically we -- or, rather, I personally spent the entire night with the soldiers who were securing the facility while Captain Paunovic was there for a while. Now, I don't know for exactly how long he was there but then he left." Have I read this out right, this statement of yours?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you talk about this, did you refer to any previous departure by Paunovic, Paunovic going anywhere else, or does this statement show that he was with you during that night for a certain period of time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The essence of this statement is to show you how concerned both the commander and I were, in view of many unknowns that we were facing and that were related to our task. In this statement, I said that for the most part of that night he was there at the gatehouse; he was with me. If they asked me whether he was coming and going, I would have told them about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You can have a look at your statement, but can we agree that you did not say that anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not deem it necessary to say that. I repeat to you yet again that the point was that we were expressing our fears in view of the number of people there. The company commander practically took part in providing this security.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Simic, we are going to move on to the morning of the 20th. You said that on the previous day, the previous evening, you had received your orders, specifically with the order to search people. Did I understand you properly that your commander was not present when you started searching these persons?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he came later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can we agree that in the morning you did not receive any instructions from him in terms of the searches, that it was done on the previous evening, as you said?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did anybody else on that morning explain to you how this was supposed to be done, or did you know from this order what was supposed to be done and whether you did what you did -- what you told us about, the line-up of the soldiers, the tables, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for anyone to issue any additional orders to me or to give me explanations because in the evening, we, Captain Paunovic and I that is, I said at the very outset that I was his deputy otherwise, and we had agreed on the entire methodology of our work, the organisation involved, how many people we needed, all of it. Everything was fully dealt with in detail, so he had no need to come earlier in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. And then you explained how this was done, that groups of about 50 people went out of the hospital, that you searched them, and that you took every one of these groups to the bus; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic asked you about this and then you personally talked about this or, rather, you said this to these people, that everybody should give their firearms or other weapons like knives, but he also asked you whether valuables were also handed in and whether you asked them to do that and your answer was no. But I'm asking you about this, some of the witnesses who had been searched said that money and valuables were taken away from them. Was that possible in view of your presence? Were you checking your own soldiers there? Can you comment these statements that were made here during these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Were those witnesses searched by my soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that these were witnesses who went to these buses. Well, I assume there weren't any other soldiers except for those that you commanded.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers I commanded did not take away any valuables from anyone, gold, jewellery, nothing. I personally stood there five metres away from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. That was precisely my question. So you were there checking this entire operation throughout, and it was impossible, if I understand you correctly, for anyone to abuse his authority and perhaps do something like that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was absolutely impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you took them to the bus, you mentioned that you remember only Major Vukasinovic from amongst the officers, but that there were other officers, too, who you cannot remember. As for these other soldiers, or, rather, officers, do you no longer remember them simply because your memory doesn't serve you any longer on account of that, or perhaps are these soldiers -- or, rather, officers who you did not know because they did not belong to the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I said perhaps there were others, but I only knew Major Vukasinovic, so I talked to him. I did say that there were others. I said perhaps there were others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You talked about Todorovic coming that morning with a reinforcement, with soldiers, right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Who commanded him on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as Captain Paunovic was my superior officer, Second Lieutenant Todorovic was then standing in for the company commander who had been wounded during combat. So Second Lieutenant Todorovic was also subordinated to Captain Paunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. I understand, then, that Paunovic was both his superior and yours. Who commanded these soldiers who were brought in as a reinforcement?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I commanded the soldiers who were attached to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, did your commander, Paunovic, come during the operation of searching and taking these people to the buses?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that he came around 9.00, he came a bit later. He didn't come when it all started.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: There was this question that had to do with the security of the buses. So if I remember correctly, you did not provide your own military policemen for this kind of job?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: However, if a witness before this Tribunal, your commander, Paunovic, said that he assigned two military policemen for each and every bus respectively, where did they come from if they didn't come from your unit? Can you answer?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paunovic was battalion commander and he had four companies of the military police under him. I was the commander only of one company. Now, from which company out of the remaining three he appointed these soldiers for accompanying the buses, if he did that, I really don't know. I just know that from my unit, there weren't any soldiers who were escorting the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I assume, on the basis of your answer, that you never talked about that and never received any information about that from your commander, Paunovic. My next question: I think you said today that all of this ended around 10.00. Could you explain this a bit better, what was it that ended around 10.00, in your view?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My task, my assignment ended around 10.00. And my task was to search these persons, and that was the end of my task. So that's what happened around 10.00, up to 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your task was to search these persons and, as you explained, to take them to the buses and to hand them over so that they would be there on the buses?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was all of that over by around 10.00?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So after that, you had no business there. You searched these persons, other persons no longer went out of the hospital, so you had no task -- or, rather, you withdrew from there, if I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That part of the task was over, the search was over, and I still had the task of providing security.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I think that you said today that you do not remember when it was that these buses set off. I think that you even said that you didn't see them leaving; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't remember when it was that they finally left and how many of them were there, and when they ultimately departed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Since you were still providing security, you and your soldiers, is it logical to assume that you would have noticed if these buses had stayed on for an unusually long time after you had accomplished your task. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe you are right, but a person who would be saying the contrary would be equally right. If I complete my duty, then somebody else is probably responsible for another -- for this other part of the task and then this other person thinks about that. I finished my task and I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. But the buses were nearby. How far away were these buses from the place where you were searching these persons?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said up to 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So can we agree that you could see that, that that was within the scope of your vision?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not standing in the same place all the time while I was there. I had to see my own people. It doesn't mean that I was just standing there. I returned the people who had conducted the searches. I went and toured my company. I saw my soldiers who were providing security. It wasn't that I was a static feature there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I agree, but that is precisely why I said a moment ago if you were coming and going that you certainly would have noticed, after a while, that the buses were there if they were still there. That is something that could not have escaped you if you are there walking around the hospital. That's my assumption, but am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say that I didn't notice any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said today that the buses or, rather, those leaving the hospital were on the left-hand side. Looking from the hospital entrance, they were headed left, and it was on the left, looking from the hospital entrance, that the buses were. Right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The emergency ward entrance, imagine yourself leaving the hospital. To your left, on that street are the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Indeed. You were still securing the hospital when those other people were leaving. You mentioned the civilians leaving and the patients and so on and so forth. Where were they heading? Were they all heading to the same side or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one detail: There were two different exits. You have the main entrance to the hospital. It was there that members of the medical staff and those who could move were evacuated. Those who couldn't walk were stretchered out of the building. I'm talking about the other evacuation. Those who couldn't walk were stretchered out the emergency exit and they were placed into ambulances. Some of them went one way and the others went the other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: One way and the other way. Where exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I talked about before, where the buses were, that's where the ambulances headed to, those carrying patients who were unable to move. They took that gate out. And the civilians being evacuated took the other gate. Or, rather, medical staff and those patients who were still able to walk.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned Karan today, didn't you? You said he was there to get Vesna Bosanac. You were there, he was outside the entrance and he never actually entered the hospital, right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I took it to mean he told you that he was there to get Vesna Bosanac. Just on whose orders, did he share that with you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He probably did. But was it the commander's orders or someone else's, I can hardly say. I know he came and then we went as far as the entrance together. They called her and -- I've given a fairly detailed account of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know whether Major Tesic had any contacts with Vesna Bosanac or that he was the one who took her to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps before my arrival, as I said, I found Major Tesic at the hospital when I arrived and he had set up some sort of security before my arrival. But whether he took Dr. Bosanac anywhere during this period of time and before our security system was in place is not something that I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I understand about before your arrival; you don't know about what happened before you came. But after your arrival, do you know about Major Tesic taking Dr. Bosanac anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know whether they, and I mean Vesna Bosanac or possibly Marin Vidic, Bili, returned to the hospital that night?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And when, as you say, Paunovic returned for the second time from Negoslavci, was Vidic not with him?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second time, which second time are you talk about? He was off to Negoslavci for that briefing. He was back from the briefing. He took Mr. Vidic with him and led him away. After that, he returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That's the time I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about the next day? Was Vidic brought to the hospital at any time during your time there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't see that gentleman. I can hardly say whether I saw him return. I didn't know him from Adam. He was taken away at a time when I was away. Therefore, I could hardly have seen him, could I?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I have only a couple of questions left for you. At page 27 today you said that you had submitted a verbal report to the commander. You said, "I can assume who that commander was," but it's not stated specifically. So who was this, for the sake of the record?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my own battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Paunovic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just another question. You've talked at great length about something that happened on the 14th of -- on the 4th of November, 1991. Can we agree that you haven't mentioned this in your previous statements? Why did you believe it to be a matter of particular importance, then?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never talked about this because nobody asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You said today that on the evening of the 19th, except for Captain Mladen Karan turning up, none of the soldiers went into or out of the hospital, right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Later on you were Captain Radic's commander, weren't you, after that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you know who he is, right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On the evening of the 19th, did you see Captain Radic anywhere at all?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, one thing that wasn't reflected in the transcript is that he was his commander after Vukovar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of November, 1991, while conducting the search and taking people to the buses, were you in any sort of contact with Captain Radic in the sense of him helping you along, giving orders, or carrying out any sort of orders at all?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he involved in taking these people to the buses in any way at all or in selecting these people or separating them off?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your own commander, Paunovic, at the time was about 55; he's testified already. We know that he was born in 1956. How tall is he; can you say?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 175 [Realtime transcript read in error: "155"] centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he sport a moustache at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's always sported one, ever since I first met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The transcript says 155 centimetres, whereas the witness said 175. I think that -- so how tall was he?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, 175 centimetres. He's slightly shorter than I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When people are being searched, selected and taken to those buses, was anyone wearing a bordeaux colour or red beret? Was anyone wearing that sort of a head-gear?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I remember, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What if somebody was wearing a head-gear of that sort? Do you think you'd remember?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It probably would have been quite easy to spot because most people on the scene were wearing helmets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were in the Vukovar theatre of war, did you have a left-hand neighbour, since you were in Assault Detachment 2, right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The left-hand neighbour was Assault Detachment 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you specifically have any sort of communication with someone who was your left-hand neighbour, a unit that was not an active unit of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a group from the Territorial Defence led, I believe, by Stanko Vujanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber received a copy of your statement from the Belgrade Ovcara trial from Mr. Domazet, the OTP have that, page 28, and the English is 57. The presiding judge asked you and Stanko Vujanovic asked you about that. You explained the reasons for there being a left neighbour and right neighbour and what the communication between these two neighbouring units was. I won't be reading that now. And then the president of the chamber said after you had stated that Stanko Vujanovic was your left neighbour, called for you to explain that, and Stanko Vujanovic asked you: "Well, of course he was in communication with me. The five or seven of us or, rather, up to 10 of us who were up front all the time, and Mr. Stamatovic, who was with his soldiers, said it himself. He kept an eye on his own soldiers rather than anything else. "Mr. Simke" - and he means you - "could not talk to him as a non-commissioned officer. He should have talked to me because I was there in front. Those of us who were ahead, and the soldiers, at least in the area where I was, were guarding certain positions that we had achieved. Of course Mr. Simic was communicating with me, not with Bojkovski or with Zoran who was 50 or 100 metres behind. Who would he communicate with?" Then a series of answers that you provided, but after all, you say that you did communicate with him and that he was the commander of that group. My question is: As you were involved in this coordinated action, as the presiding judge asked you, along that particular axis, how far to your left was Stanko Vujanovic and the group that he was in command of?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only one street between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that behind that group at a distance of between 50 and 100 metres, there were regular troops with their company commanders?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say. I said back then that I didn't know about the exact disposition of Assault Detachment 1. I joined the fray there as a replacement for the anti-terrorist company. I took up those positions and I never moved in order to cross to the other side. We didn't budge over those 10 days, not an inch.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Is it true that the only left neighbour you had was Stanko Vujanovic's group, the group that he was in command of, and they were not regular troops or commanders, right, not within their combat disposition?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see a single soldier of ours or officer of ours with Stanko Vujanovic and his group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please be so kind and try to remember when you were deployed along that axis. First of all, what were those people wearing that Stanko Vujanovic was in command of?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see much of them. Stanko would normally wear a black hat, a black coat. Normally, I say. Whenever I saw him, he would wear that sort of thing, that sort of clothes. I didn't see much of the rest of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Along your own axis of operations --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please go into private session for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are no open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This concludes my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Moore, you could run now for about a quarter of an hour or have a break now, whichever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I run for 15 minutes and then take a break? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you still have breath after 15 minutes running, Mr. Moore, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, when one talks about your evidence and the accounts that you have given to courts, both here and Serbia, would I be right in generalising in the following way, that what you're saying is in 1999 and 2005 you considered and expressed the view that Sljivancanin was in charge of not only the matters on the 19th but also the evacuation on the 20th, but since coming to The Hague and speaking to associates, you have come to a different conclusion, that he was not in charge. Is that the nub of your evidence on that topic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am testifying about events that took place. I talk about the way I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the question is perfectly easy. You make a statement in 1999 to a court; 2005 you do the same. Dealing with this topic about command, the suggestion is in that statement in 1999 and 2005, you're saying Sljivancanin is in charge. You come, basically to The Hague, having spoken to some friends, and you seem to be suggesting that Sljivancanin was not in charge. Now, is that right or not, or do you say as far as you remember, Sljivancanin was in charge on the 19th and the 20th? And please remember you are on oath.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying that I got my tasks from Captain Paunovic, and I'm saying that I saw Major Sljivancanin there as well. For example, specifically, as for the 20th, he came in the morning, he greeted me, and he entered the hospital. Now, what he did in the hospital and what he was responsible for, that is something I really don't know. However, as for what I was responsible for and what I did, I know about that, but I assert that I did not enter the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you a question about entering the hospital. I am asking you about the impression that you gathered on the 19th and 20th of November, 1991. Was Sljivancanin, the impression that you got, that Sljivancanin was in charge on the 19th and on the 20th? Now, it's a simple question. It's the third time I've asked it. Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, I cannot respond what my impression was at that time. I'm talking about facts, I'm not talking about impressions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would suggest to you that is not correct. You are perfectly entitled to draw impressions of what you saw in 1991 and come to a conclusion. Whether it is right or wrong may be a separate issue, but is the impression that you gathered that Sljivancanin was in charge on the 19th and 20th? These are two separate issues.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then, in that statement in 2005 that you've probably read -- in that statement from 2005, I said that I think that Major Sljivancanin was in charge of that part of the operation; that is to say, what is going on within the hospital compound. That is the impression that I had at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it is not just 2005, it is also 1999 that you formed that impression as well. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, you have seen Mr. Lukic, two, if not three times. I have absolutely no doubt, whether it was Mr. Bulatovic or Mr. Lukic that you have seen these statements, and I'd suggest that topic was dealt with, wasn't it? So it's not probably, the answer is you know perfectly well that's what you said in both those statements; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, will that be an appropriate moment. I know it's a little earlier than I anticipated, but I will deal with other matters and I'd prefer to deal with it in toto, if Your Honour wouldn't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at quarter to, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So Mr. Simic, the impression that you gathered was that Sljivancanin was in charge; that is correct. You have already agreed to that. Now, what I want to ask you is this: What were the characteristics, what was the behaviour of Major Sljivancanin that made you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that then, when I gave those statements, I had that impression. Now, why did I have this impression? Because out of all persons present there in the hospital compound, as this event was taking place, the most senior-ranking person was Major Sljivancanin. That is how I had that assumption. However, the chain of command is clearly defined. My commander was my battalion commander and he issued orders to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I am not asking about orders being issued to you. That is not the question. I'm talking about the operation itself, the evacuation. Isn't it right that the view that you took was that Mr. Sljivancanin was in charge of the entire operation? That was the view, whether it's right or wrong, that was the view you took; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in my statement before the special court. But obviously then I didn't understand the prosecutor either -- or, rather, the president of the court and he didn't understand me either. I presented my impression then in relation to what happened in the hospital, that Sljivancanin was responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm going to go through the two documents that were compiled as a result of your interviews in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know the documents have come in before Your Honour, but for my reference purposes, may I ask the Court to look at a compiled bundle that we have created which is almost identical to my learned friend's, but the references are slightly different. The Court should have them and we have got copies for the Defence, if they require them, but I know they have already got the bundles. Could the witness please be given a hard copy. I see Mr. Borovic looking concerned. Can I just indicate that it's exactly the same documents as given by my learned friend on behalf of Mr. Mrksic, just the indexing slightly different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, let me explain how this file is built; it's really very simple. There are four tab numbers, 1, 2, 3, and 4. There is an index at the front. Item 1, or tab 1, is in English; 2 is the B/C/S translation of it, or perhaps it's the other way around; 3 is the English transcript for the later hearing in July 2005; and number four is the original transcript. So I want to deal, if I may, please, with this topic in the following way. What were you doing in the latter part of 1995, just in general terms? I think it's right that you had a promotion or you left the Guards in 1995, I think September the 9th, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995, I was not in the Guards Brigade. On the 6th of June, 1994, the 46th Protection Motorised Brigade was established and I then became commander of the battalion of the military police of that brigade. I think that in September 1995 I was a desk officer in the operations and teaching department because I was about to start school. However, due to what happened in Operation Storm, the school was put off for the beginning of 1996. So this school, that is to say, the staff college, started for me in 1996. That's when I enrolled -- yes, what was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What I have - and you can confirm whether it's right or not - from the 5th of April, 1993, until the 8th of September, 1995, you were the commander of the Guards Brigade military police battalion, Belgrade garrison. Does that sound familiar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, I was not the commander of the brigade. I was commander of the battalion. Commander of the battalion that was not within the Guards Brigade. At first, it was within the 46th Regiment for providing security, and then within the 46th Protection Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In any event, in 1995, we know that indictments were issued in relation to this case for Mr. Mrksic, Mr. Sljivancanin, and Mr. Radic and that that fact was publicised in the press. Now, were you aware of an indictment, not obviously the particulars, but the fact that an indictment had been issued against these three gentlemen?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that I learned about that through the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I'm suggesting 1995, would that be correct, approximately? I'm not going to worry about months here or there.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. The answer is probably yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. So the situation came that on the 15th of January, 1999, you were called before the Belgrade military court; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And as I say, it's the 15th of January. How much notice were you given that you were going to have to be giving evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can I put it this way: Clearly giving evidence before an investigating judge of the military court in Belgrade in respect of the war crimes committed, as we would say, at Ovcara, is an extremely and was an extremely serious event for you; do you agree with that? Not to be taken lightly.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I didn't take it lightly. But now I cannot say whether I received the summons 15, 20 days earlier, or a month earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the one thing is certain is that you knew that you were going to be asked about an evacuation that you had played a part at the beginning. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is something that I only could have assumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You knew perfectly well that, not from your own personal knowledge, but the suggestion was that there was an inquiry being made about the people who had been killed at Ovcara. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you came to give your evidence, the learned judge informed you of various obligations and rights. Now, I'm going to ask you, please, to go to divider 2, which I hope is pink but may not be pink, and you will find, I hope, on page 02188239 in the B/C/S, page 2 at the bottom of the English version, the following phrase, and I don't want to waste much time on it: "Within the meaning of Article 229 of the Law on Criminal Procedure, the witness has been informed that: He does not have to answer questions if there is a likelihood that by doing so he would expose himself or a close relative to serious humiliation, considerable material damage or criminal prosecution." And the next below it: "Within the meaning of Article 231 of the Law on Criminal Procedure, the witness has been reminded that he is under obligation to tell the truth and not to withhold any information since giving false testimony constitutes a criminal offence, and that he was also under obligation to inform the court about any change of address or residence." It's something that we have seen before. So the learned judge is telling you what your rights are: Tell the truth, but if there's something that might incriminate you, you don't have to say anything. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And so when it came to this particular interview, you were being asked to make a statement about what you knew that had occurred on the 19th and 20th, perhaps even the 21st of November, 1991. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to take up a lot of time dealing with the material at the start. What I would suggest is you indicate that your battalion commander at that time was Captain Paunovic. There was reference to Ovcara, but not in the sense that we know it. There is then reference to "the actual town of Vukovar being taken by our units as part of the lifting of the blockade." That is on English page 4 at the top; and the B/C/S page is 02188240. Now I want to deal from that section, if I may. "The actual town of Vukovar was taken by our units as part of the lifting of the blockade of Vukovar barracks and liberating imprisoned civilians in Vukovar. If I remember correctly, Vukovar was taken on the 18th of November, 1991, in the afternoon." So I would suggest, there you are, you've got the date pretty much spot on. You then indicate you're between two streets. "And after that, I was given the task of carrying out search and investigation of the terrain in the Mitnica area in order to check if there were any remnants of left-over units of the opposing side." So that is what you have told this Court today; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Then you go on. You say: "While I was carrying out the task, as I remember it today, it may have been the 19th of November, I was given an order from the battalion commander to go urgently with my company to the hospital sector in Vukovar, so I arrived with my company from the Mitnica area between 1400 and 1500 hours. When I arrived in front of the hospital in Vukovar, I found the battalion commander Paunovic and Major Sljivancanin." So again, entirely consistent with the evidence that you have given today. You get the date correct, the fact that you are called to go from Mitnica, that you go there, the timing is pretty much correct, and there you find Paunovic and Sljivancanin. That's right, isn't it? That's right, Mr. Simic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that it was right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just going to go through the statement. And then there is reference to Tesic. Turning over the page to page 5, English, and it's the B/C/S version of -- towards the end of 02188240, you said: "I had not known Captain Radic until then because I came to the unit later so I don't know whether he was there providing security at the hospital or not." You then proceed to say about providing security, not allowing anyone to enter or leave. "However, in the hospital perimeter, there were many people, civilians, as well as population, so through the organisation of senior officers from the brigade command, and I think that Major Sljivancanin was in charge of that, they left the hospital perimeter on foot and they departed." Just dealing with that aspect of evidence. It's right, isn't it, you said that you had a discussion with Tesic. It's right that you made reference to Radic. It's been dealt with here. And the fact that you were providing security and you would not allow anyone to leave -- enter or leave the hospital premises, that is correct, that's entirely consistent with your evidence, isn't it, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And so when we come to the final part of that paragraph, "I think that Major Sljivancanin was in charge of that, they left the hospital perimeter on foot and they departed." What do you mean "of that"? What's the phrase "of that" refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that, I said in that same sentence -- yes, just a moment, please. Sorry, let me just read it once again. "Of that," meant that the departure of civilians who left the hospital perimeter on that day meaning that as they departed, I thought then, as it's written here, that Major Sljivancanin was in charge of that. That's what I thought -- again, I'm talking about impressions because I told you who was there at that moment: Major Sljivancanin, Captain Paunovic and Major Tesic. Out of all of them, Major Sljivancanin was the most senior-ranking officer and hence my assumption that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My apologies. But can I also suggest that when one comes to an assumption about behaviour, it's not just about rank in the army, it's also the way people behave; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could not agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So are you saying, then, that you come to that collusion, "I think Major Sljivancanin was in charge of that," purely because of his rank?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That being the case, what was it that Sljivancanin was doing at that time? Because you used phrase "they departed," so I'd like to know what Mr. Sljivancanin was doing. Will you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that on that day this team of the International Committee of the Red Cross came, too, and that he talked to them on that occasion and that he gave me some guidelines. I already told you that. I also did other things. I told you that. I was not paying attention only to what Sljivancanin was doing. Quite simply, from among all the persons I encounter there, knowing the persons from the brigade command, he was the only one there; hence, my logical assumption that he was probably the one in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So he was an officer, the most senior officer from the brigade command at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of those that I saw, the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Then why do you use the phrase "senior officers," plural?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Major Tesic and Captain Paunovic were there, too, while I was there, too. And I'm saying that in relation to those who were present there, he was the man who held the highest rank in the brigade command from among all of those who were present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But what do you mean by the phrase "through the organisation of senior officers"? What organisation? What was occurring? What was being organised?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't some big organisation. Quite simply, what was stated was that persons who were not from the hospital, namely who were not employed at the hospital and who were not patients at the hospital, could leave the hospital on that day. It's not some organisation that's involved there. People would simply leave as we opened the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But we are talking, are we not, about groups of people leaving the hospital and the hospital area? And I'm asking you what organisation? What was being done at that time in respect of that? Because you used the phrase "through the organisation of senior officers." It's not my phrase; it's your phrase.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we talking about the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I sincerely hope so, because that's what I've been referring you to.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Then we are talking about the same thing. I'm telling you that there wasn't any need for specially organising these activities. Quite simply, people were allowed, without any restrictions, without any checks, to leave. Only if they were patients in the hospital or if they were employees of the hospital, it was different. As far as I can remember now, I was just supposed to channel these people, so to speak, towards the main entrance to the hospital compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But didn't you hear that there was going to be an evacuation from Velepromet of civilians at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for what happened in Velepromet, I had nothing whatsoever to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That is not what I asked. I asked quite simply: Did you not know there was going to be an evacuation from Velepromet and that the civilians should go in that general area?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not quite understand what you said just now. Are you asking me whether I knew that these civilians were supposed to go to Velepromet and that from Velepromet they would be evacuated further on or whether I knew at all where they were going?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, didn't you think to yourself, Where on earth are these people going to go? Hadn't it been mentioned by anyone that there was, what I will call, a clearance facility, a refugee facility, at Velepromet? Are you saying you didn't know that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said that I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So is it right that you knew about Velepromet being the base for civilians being evacuated in due course?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And is it not right to say that you got that information from that group of officers, including Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot really answer that because I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us move on to your statement, just continuing. I'm going to call that evacuation one, if I may, just for convenience. I hope it will be obvious in due course why. Next paragraph: "The next day, it may have been the 20th of November, I was given the task by the battalion commander to organise the search of persons who were being led out of the hospital where some classification and sorting had been done." Then you go on to say: "... so we set up some tables in front of the hospital and people came from the hospital in groups." Now, is that correct, in general terms?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had received the task on the previous day. Here I was talking about the task that I was carrying out on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In general terms, is it right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is right that those persons were searched on the 20th and I had received the task on the evening of the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. The task of the -- the task was given the evening of the 19th by, you said, Paunovic. Here: "I was given the task by the battalion commander," we know that's Paunovic, "... to organise the search of persons," that's correct, isn't it, "who were being led out of the hospital," we know that's correct, "where some classifications and sorting had been done, so we set up some tables in front of the hospital and people came from the hospital in groups." Simple question: In general terms, is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. Are you asking me about the entire sentence being right as such, or am I supposed to address certain parts of these sentences?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will break it into parts so there's no misunderstanding. "The next day, it may have been the 20th of November," well, you say it's the 19th, "I was given the task by the battalion commander to organise the search of persons." Now, you were given the task by the battalion commander. You've told us that Paunovic gave you such --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The previous evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what you say. I accept that. So Paunovic gave you -- he gave you the order, the task, to organise the search of persons. You agree with that; yes?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. "Who were being led out of the hospital." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "Where some classification and sorting had been done." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A triage, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, classification and sorting had been done. Can we say triage reflects that? Triage is the selection, normally.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that was done back at the hospital; that is, inside the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the phrase "where some classification and sorting had been done," you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. "So we set up some tables in front of the hospital." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "And people came from the hospital in groups." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us just deal, then, with the next, because I will come back to that. "These were people between 20 and 40 years of age who were all in civilian clothes." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "And some of them had leather Macloud jackets on." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people wearing such jackets, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. "About which we later found out had been given to them as assistance and were in fact used so they could change." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were our assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to deal with this phrase which you now accept is correct. I want to ask you about the phrase at the very start, about: "To organise the search of persons who were being led out of the hospital where some classification and sorting had been done." Now the classification and sorting, I want to just focus on that topic. All right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us in your evidence that Sljivancanin came in the morning of the 20th, and he came with a group of officers because you refer to -- you could see the rank. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And there was a second group of doctors in uniform; that is also correct. That was your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with the first group, please, not the doctors, what I will call the non-doctors group. So what ranks are we talking about? Officer ranks, obviously, but are we able to establish what sort of ranks?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite remember those people or their ranks. I don't know if all of them were officers; maybe some of them were NCOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But with regard to the officers, you've told us that some of them were officers, because you could see their badge, where did those officers come from, which units? Because clearly, you were in charge of security, and you must have been curious to know who it was that was coming in to your area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know those people. I didn't notice. I probably did notice. It's just that I don't remember now what their ranks were. It's only to be expected that if a chief of security of a brigade is entering there is no need to ID any of the people accompanying him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Clearly, Paunovic had gone to a briefing at, I think it's 6.00, of OG South on the 19th; that is right, isn't it? You've told us about that, he went at 5.00, 5.30?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was told. He told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And clearly, here is -- from what you seem to be saying is, here is the chief of the security organ of OG South coming to the hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And with regard to that, can I just deal with the other group of people, the doctors. How many doctors were there, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were about four or five doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And so when you say about sorting out, what was being used to sort out the people in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say, because I wasn't there. I have said several times that I never entered the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you were briefed the night before by Paunovic and a briefing has a purpose. It specifically tells the individual what their task is. The briefing with Paunovic, were you the only officer at that briefing?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was also Captain Majkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So two officers there for the briefing, no more?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So what was the other officer's task?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other officer was assistant commander for moral guidance with the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But what were you told about the purpose of the filtering system? There must have been a reason to say, Well, some are going here; some are going there; we are looking for. There has to be a rationale explained to you so you understand what your task is. So in general terms, what was the rationale of this briefing?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The task was precisely set out to me. I was to line up any persons leaving the hospital and frisk them with the remaining soldiers. I was to search them for any blunt objects or firearms. Having searched the group, I was to take them as far as the buses. My task -- or, rather, I knew nothing at all about how the work inside -- how work inside the hospital was organised or what the respective responsibilities were inside the hospital. My task involving those people only began once they had left the hospital building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You had no women soldiers with you, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I'm living in a -- or we're all living in a period of political correctness, but what was going to happen if ladies were coming along? Who was going to be doing the searching of them to see whether they are carrying sharp implements?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no women -- women were not frisked. If there had been any women, we probably would not have frisked anyone, anyway. It was envisaged that only female persons could frisk any other female persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So can we assume that what was expected was that it would be men coming through, not women?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't even assume. I hope you understand what I mean. Whatever was envisaged or done inside the hospital was nothing to do with my task. My sole task was searching those persons. You referred to women. If there had been any such cases, we would probably have gone and fetched a nurse or a female doctor from inside the hospital to frisk that particular person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to go on with your statement. I'll just read it out, and I'd suggest it's almost identical to what your evidence is. It reads as follows, the English page 5, three-fifths of the way down the page. For the assistance of the witness, it is page 021882240. "These men were searched to check if they had any weapons on them or similar, and after the search, escorted by the soldiers from my unit, they were loaded onto the buses that were at the hospital entrance gate. After they got on the buses, they were driven somewhere. I do not know where these people were driven in buses because I was not interested nor was I informed. The task of my unit was only to carry out the search of these people and load them on the bus, nothing else." Now, can I perhaps suggest to you that this tranche of evidence pretty much reflects what you have said in evidence. There is no significant difference at all. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I need another look. You could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I do. Now, let's just move on, if we may. "Throughout this time, while we were providing security and carried out the searches, none of my soldiers entered the hospital premises until the evacuation was complete." Can I put it that way also, that that corresponds with your account in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Reading on, I'm nearly finished. "During the search, no register was kept, nor were lists made of people taken out of the hospital and their loading onto the buses. I do not know whether anyone had kept a record in the hospital before this." Can I deal with it this way, and I may come back to it, but as far as you're concerned and in the evidence you gave, you didn't compile a list. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So your evidence in relation to this statement is almost 100 per cent a mirror. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, not roughly speaking. I'd suggest it's much more than roughly speaking; it's almost 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to deal with the next passage. "As far as I was able to see, all the tasks in relation to the organisation were handled by Major Veselin Sljivancanin, and my battalion commander Paunovic was also there." Now, we have heard your evidence, now let's just look at this phrase: "As far as I was able to see, all the tasks ..." So can we take it, then, that when you use the phrase "as far as I was able to see ..." that means from what you could see at that time, you came to the conclusion, whether right or wrong, that all the tasks in relation to the organisation were handled by Sljivancanin with Paunovic also being there. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true, Paunovic was there. It's also true, I repeat, as I said in reference to the impressions that you mentioned, given the fact that there was no other person from the brigade command who was more senior or holding a higher ranking position than Major Sljivancanin, I assumed that what was being done at the hospital or what we were doing outside the hospital was something that he was in charge [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, I will come back to that, but I want to move on, if I may, to -- Perhaps in fairness to you -- when you made this phrase, it was in relation to the entire evacuation; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all right, that's a different statement. That's the one for the special court where I said that I thought he was in charge of the entire operation. But it's quite clear that there was a misunderstanding between me and the presiding judge. As I said in my previous statement, as for any activities going on inside or outside the hospital, Sljivancanin was in charge. Or, rather, I apologise, there was no way I could possibly have assumed that he was in charge of an entire operation, some operation, since I was not familiar with any other elements of that operation. I think there was a misunderstanding when the question first occurred at the special court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I suggest there's absolutely no misunderstanding at all. In your first statement, you say "able to see all the tasks," you're quite specific about it, "all the tasks," and when it comes to -- and I'll ask the Court perhaps if they would be kind enough to turn to divider 3; for you, Mr. Simic, divider 4. For the English, it is page 29, bottom of the page, that's for the English version; and for the B/C/S, it's 0461-9798. So if you go to divider 4, Mr. Simic, and the English speakers actually go to page 28 and then I'll move into 29 as well, we can deal with that very specific point. So page 28 and the page number for you is 0461-9798 but for the English speakers 28. "Presiding judge: "So at the very beginning" -- this is at the bottom of page 28. "So at the very beginning, when you arrived?" Deputy Prosecutor, Dusan Knezevic: "Who was in charge of - he said something about this subject, so let's turn to it - screening and organising the transport of these people by from the hospital onward?" "Onward." Page 29 English: "Witness Simic: As far as I was concerned, my battalion commander was in charge, and I think that Major Sljivancanin was in charge of the entire operation." It's page 28/29 of the English, divider 3. I hope the Court have got that. Would Your Honour forgive me, I may have a spare bundle if the pages have been missed. My apologies if there is an error in the machine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have found, we believe, the right page, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I just go over it again so that there's no misunderstanding in fairness to the witness, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, the page for you should be 0461-9798. The English should be bottom page 28 and 29. The question was asked -- thank you. "So who was in charge of - he said something about this subject, so let's turn to it - screening and organising the transport of these persons by from the hospital onward?" Note the word "onward." Witness, that's you, Mr. Simic: "As far as I was concerned, my battalion commander was in charge, and I think that Major Sljivancanin was in charge of the entire operation." So I want to deal with this answer: Paunovic was your commander. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And he was in charge of you. You were subordinated to him?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And so when you actually refer to "my battalion commander was in charge," that relates to you, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you make the reply that you think that Sljivancanin was in charge of the entire operation, what that means is over and above Paunovic. That's correct, isn't it? That was what you thought at the time.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us just go back, then, to divider 1 again, the original statement made by you on the 15th of January, 1999. There is reference to finding ammunition; I'm not going to go into that. But there is a paragraph just below that paragraph that we have been talking about about Mr. Sljivancanin overseeing all the tasks. "After their evacuation" -- it's page 6 of the English, tab 1, three-fifths of the way down the page. "After their evacuation, an evacuation of sick and wounded was carried out, organised by the medical personnel and the Medecins sans Frontieres team. My unit did not take part in this but we continued to provide security for the hospital perimeter." And you agree that is what happened; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The ill, the wounded, and the medical staff were evacuated. I mentioned it in my evidence today. I didn't press the point. But we were there to help things along, if needed, and we did, in some cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to move on to the B/C/S page 0218-8242; it is the English page 7, tab 1. So your page 0218-8242. Have you got that? It should start --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- "while we were guarding the hospital and its perimeter" - have you got that? - "there were cases that some locals, civilians and even some in some uniforms tried to enter the hospital saying that there were men in hospital who were sheltering there and who had killed a member of someone's family, and these people now wanted to go in and settle the scores. However, in spite of their forceful insistence, the security did not let them go in. I could not say for sure how many such cases there were, but there were quite a few. Considering the situation in Vukovar as a whole, the way it was for me and my soldiers, this was a normal reaction of these people, so to speak." I want to deal with this area of your evidence. What you are saying there, I'd suggest, almost accurately reflects what you have said today, that there was hostility around the hospital on the 19th. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A hostile atmosphere, perhaps yes, but no acts of hostility. I said then and I said today that there were taunts, verbal acts of provocation, but no use of physical force or physical attacks or indeed use of weapons. Those forms of behaviour did not occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But one of the things that was being said was "there were people in there, in the hospital, who may have killed relatives of mine." That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
